en.name: Cuthbert
en.summary: Beloved seventh-century monk-bishop of Lindisfarne who preferred solitary island hermitage but was repeatedly called back into pastoral leadership.
en.body: Cuthbert entered monastic life in northern England as a young man, reportedly after a vision on the night Bishop Aidan of Lindisfarne died, and became renowned across the region for his tireless pastoral work, traveling to remote and difficult mountain villages that other clergy avoided to preach and minister personally to isolated communities. Despite this evident gift for pastoral leadership, he was repeatedly drawn toward solitary contemplative life, eventually withdrawing to live as a hermit on the tiny, wind-battered Farne Islands, only to be persuaded, with considerable reluctance, to accept appointment as Bishop of Lindisfarne when the king and church leadership insisted his gifts were too valuable to leave in solitude. He resigned the bishopric after only two years to return to his island hermitage, where he died in 687. His body was later found remarkably preserved when exhumed, and devotion to him became one of the most significant cults of early medieval England, with his shrine, eventually relocated to Durham Cathedral, remaining a major site of pilgrimage.
